content: Rifaximin is indicated for the treatment of travelers' diarrhea caused by noninvasive strains of Escherichia coli (E. coli). For this condition, the recommended dosage is 200 mg taken orally every 8 hours for 3 days. It is also used for the maintenance of remission in patients with irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhea (IBS-D), with a dosage of 550 mg taken orally every 12 hours. For IBS-D, the treatment course is 550 mg orally every 8 hours for 14 days, and symptoms that recur can be retreated with up to two additional 14-day courses. Rifaximin is available in unit-dose packaging containing 42 tablets, which is a 2-week supply for IBS-D treatment. However, it is not indicated or proven effective for travelers' diarrhea complicated by fever, bloody stool, or caused by pathogens other than noninvasive strains of E. coli. To minimize the development of drug-resistant bacteria and maintain antibiotic effectiveness, rifaximin should only be used for infections that are proven or strongly suspected to be bacterial in origin. The safety and efficacy of rifaximin for travelers' diarrhea in children under 12 years of age have not been established. For individuals aged 12 years and older, the recommended dosage is 200 mg orally every 8 hours for 3 days, with or without food. Rifaximin interacts with several drugs, primarily through the P-glycoprotein (P-gp) efflux transporter. Many medications, such as cyclosporine, clarithromycin, and amiodarone, can increase rifaximin levels by inhibiting P-gp, necessitating caution and close monitoring. In some cases, dose adjustments of rifaximin or the interacting drug may be required. For example, coadministration of cyclosporine with rifaximin has been shown to result in an 83-fold increase in rifaximin's peak concentration (Cmax) and a 124-fold increase in its area under the curve (AUC). Certain drugs, such as lasmiditan and cholera vaccine, should be avoided or replaced with alternative therapies when used with rifaximin due to significant pharmacodynamic antagonism or reduced vaccine efficacy. Similarly, rifaximin may decrease the effectiveness of live bacterial therapies, such as oral microbiota or sodium picosulfate, by altering gut flora. Antibiotic regimens should be completed 2–4 days before initiating such therapies. Adverse effects associated with rifaximin include flatulence (11%), headache (10%), rectal tenesmus (7%), abdominal pain (7%), defecation urgency (6%), nausea (5%), constipation (4%), fever (3%), and vomiting (2%). Hypersensitivity reactions, including allergic dermatitis, pruritus, and rash, have been reported. Rare but severe adverse reactions include rhabdomyolysis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), particularly in patients with cirrhosis. Close monitoring is recommended for patients at risk of these complications.
